title: Building a Walnut Side Table With Hand Tools Only
creator: Oak & Iron Shop
description:
No power tools, no shortcuts: a small walnut side table with hand-cut mortise and tenon joints and a drawbored finish.

sentences.t: Alright, so the legs are roughed out, and now comes the part I always dread, which is the mortises.
I'm doing these by hand today, no router, just a chisel, a mallet, and a lot of patience.
The trick is to start in the middle and work your way out toward the lines.
If you start right on the line, the chisel wants to lever back and you end up with a mortise that's a sixteenth too wide.
Ask me how I know.
Okay, that's one down, seven to go.
One thing I'll say, keep paring back to your knife line every few chops, don't just bash away at the bottom.
And check your chisel is vertical from the side, because a mortise that wanders off square is really hard to fix later.
I keep a little square standing right next to the leg as a reference, it helps a lot.
I'm gonna speed this up, because nobody needs to watch me chop walnut for forty minutes.

Alright, back to the bench.
All eight mortises are chopped, and honestly, they came out cleaner than I expected.
Now for the tenons on the aprons.
I mark these off the actual mortises rather than off a ruler, because no two hand-cut mortises are ever exactly the same.
Each leg gets a number in pencil, and each apron end gets the matching number.
If you skip this step, you will spend an afternoon trying every tenon in every hole like a really sad jigsaw puzzle.
For the cheeks I'm using my rip saw, and I'm sawing a hair proud of the line.
Then I sneak up on the fit with a shoulder plane.
Listen to that, that's the sound of a plane that's actually sharp for once.
Okay, test fit.
Oh, that's nice, that's snug without needing the mallet.
You want it to go in with firm hand pressure, and you want it to stay put if you pick the whole thing up.
If it falls apart when you lift it, it's too loose, and glue is not going to save you.
Next up is drawboring, which is my favorite old-timey trick.
You drill the peg hole through the mortise first, then you assemble the joint and mark the hole on the tenon.
Then you pull it apart and drill the tenon hole about a millimeter closer to the shoulder.
So when you drive the oak peg in, it pulls the joint tight, and it'll hold even if the glue fails a hundred years from now.
Pegs are split from a scrap of white oak, not sawn, because a split peg follows the grain and won't snap.
I shave a little taper on the end so it finds its way through the offset holes.
Glue-up time, which is always the most stressful five minutes of any build.
Glue on both cheeks, tap it home, and in go the pegs.
Oh, listen to that, you can hear it pulling tight.
Square check across the diagonals, and we are within a sixteenth, which for hand tools I'll take every day.
I'll let that sit overnight, and next time we'll flatten the top and get some oil on it.
If you're building along, the plans are linked below, and let me know how your mortises turn out.
